items.title: Cardinality of power set of a finite set

question.text: Why does a finite set S with n elements have exactly 2 to the power n subsets?

from_notes.text: If a finite set \(S = \{x_1, \ldots, x_n\}\) has \(n\) elements, each element can either be included or not in a subset, giving \(2^n\) subsets.

explanation.text: Each element \(x_i\) has two independent choices: include it or exclude it. Multiplying these for all \(n\) elements gives \(2^n\) subsets in total.

answer.text: From notes

Explanation

question.text: How are the union and intersection of sets A and B defined?

from_notes.text: The union \(A \cup B\) is the set of elements in \(A\) or \(B\). The intersection \(A \cap B\) is the set of elements in both \(A\) and \(B\).

answer.text: From notes

items.title: Complement of a set with respect to a universal set U

question.text: What is the complement of a set A relative to a universal set U?

from_notes.text: The complement of \(A\) is \(A^c = U \setminus A\); it contains all elements in \(U\) not in \(A\).

answer.text: From notes

question: Can the sum of a rational number and an irrational number ever be rational?

parts: The sum of a rational and an irrational number is never rational.

items.title: Definition of a function between sets

question.text: What is the definition of a function from a set X to a set Y?

from_notes.text: A function from \(X\) to \(Y\) is a relation \(f \subset X \times Y\) such that for every \(x \in X\), there is exactly one \(y \in Y\) with \((x,y) \in f\).

explanation.text: Each element of the domain \(X\) is associated with a unique element in the codomain \(Y\), ensuring a well-defined output for each input.

answer.text: From notes
A function from \(X\) to \(Y\) is a relation \(f \subset X \times Y\) such that for every \(x \in X\), there is exactly one \(y \in Y\) with \((x,y) \in f\).
Explanation
Each element of the domain \(X\) is associated with a unique element in the codomain \(Y\), ensuring a well-defined output for each input.

items.title: Equality of functions

question.text: Under what conditions are two functions equal?

from_notes.text: Two functions \(f: X_1 \to Y_1\) and \(g: X_2 \to Y_2\) are equal if \(X_1 = X_2\) and \(f(x) = g(x)\) for all \(x \in X_1\).

explanation.text: Equality requires identical domains and matching values for all elements in the domain. The codomain equality may or may not be required depending on definitions.

Explanation

items.title: When is a function injective, surjective, and bijective?

question.text: What characterizes an injective, surjective, and bijective function from X to Y?

from_notes.text: A function \(f:X \to Y\) is: (1) injective if distinct inputs map to distinct outputs; (2) surjective if every element of \(Y\) is an image of some element in \(X\); (3) bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

explanation.text: Injectivity means no two different inputs share the same output; surjectivity means the function covers the entire codomain; bijection means a perfect one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain.

answer.text: From notes

A function \(f:X \to Y\) is: (1) injective if distinct inputs map to distinct outputs; (2) surjective if every element of \(Y\) is an image of some element in \(X\); (3) bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
Explanation

Injectivity means no two different inputs share the same output; surjectivity means the function covers the entire codomain; bijection means a perfect one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain.

items.title: What does the inverse function of a bijection represent?

question.text: What is the inverse function of a bijection and when does it exist?

from_notes.text: If \(f: X \to Y\) is a bijection, its inverse function \(f^{-1}: Y \to X\) is defined by \(f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y\).

explanation.text: The inverse function swaps the roles of inputs and outputs and exists only if \(f\) is bijective, guaranteeing each output comes from exactly one input.

answer.text: From notes

Explanation

items.title: How does image and preimage of sets under a function behave with unions and intersections?

question.text: What are the relations between images and preimages of unions and intersections of subsets under a function f?

from_notes.text: For \(f: X \to Y\), and subsets \(A,B \subset X\), \(C,D \subset Y\): (i) \(f(A \cap B) \subset f(A) \cap f(B)\), (ii) \(f(A \cup B) = f(A) \cup f(B)\), (iii) \(A \subset f^{-1}(f(A))\), (iv) \(f^{-1}(C \cap D) = f^{-1}(C) \cap f^{-1}(D)\) and (v) \(f^{-1}(C \cup D) = f^{-1}(C) \cup f^{-1}(D)\).

explanation.text: The image of a union equals the union of images, but the image of an intersection is contained in (not necessarily equal to) the intersection of images. Preimages preserve unions and intersections exactly.

answer.text: From notes

For \(f: X \to Y\), and subsets \(A,B \subset X\), \(C,D \subset Y\): (i) \(f(A \cap B) \subset f(A) \cap f(B)\), (ii) \(f(A \cup B) = f(A) \cup f(B)\), (iii) \(A \subset f^{-1}(f(A))\), (iv) \(f^{-1}(C \cap D) = f^{-1}(C) \cap f^{-1}(D)\) and (v) \(f^{-1}(C \cup D) = f^{-1}(C) \cup f^{-1}(D)\).
Explanation

The image of a union equals the union of images, but the image of an intersection is contained in (not necessarily equal to) the intersection of images. Preimages preserve unions and intersections exactly.
